description: Solo developer interested in XR and space exploration.
summary:
Mission Lens is an XR prototype for turning science objectives into observation plans before a hypothetical Marswalk. Built in Unity for Meta Quest 3, it combines NASA orbital terrain data, Perseverance panoramas, and sampling records in an Earth-based briefing.

Users move between a tabletop 3D map and ground-level views of Jezero Crater, frame images, and link each image to its scientific purpose and planned follow-up observations. The case pairs Skinner Ridge and Wildcat Ridge to investigate ancient water environments and evidence that could constrain their timing.

The saved briefing records where to look, why it matters, and what remains unresolved, providing a plan for review and discussion. Historical NASA observations, our calculations, and planned observations remain clearly distinguished.
details:
Purpose

Mission Lens turns a science objective into a visual observation plan for a hypothetical Marswalk in Jezero Crater. The intended user is a crew scientist preparing an Earth-based briefing: where should we look, what should we record, and what will remain unresolved?

A science case grounded in rover research

The case pairs Skinner Ridge and Wildcat Ridge. Wildcat Ridge’s fine-grained, sulfate- and clay-bearing rocks record an ancient water environment and have potential to preserve ancient organic material. Skinner Ridge’s coarser, diverse grains offer complementary opportunities for future laboratory analyses that could constrain geological timing. These published findings inform our observation-planning scenario. Connecting them requires documenting their geological context; numerical ages cannot be read from a panorama or terrain height. Bosak et al. (2024) (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024AV001241).

How it works

PLAN: The user explores a tabletop 3D terrain map, reviews the outcrops’ geology and NASA sampling records, and assigns each site a role in the observation plan.

FIELD: The user enters the corresponding Mastcam-Z panorama, looks around, and frames a view with a virtual camera. A capture retains its station, viewing direction, image source, and observation purpose. From that image, the user can plan a close-up with scale, a wider context image, or another viewpoint. These remain future observations. Archived WATSON close-ups are available as separate rover evidence.

RETURN AND SAVE: Back at the table, the photographs stay linked to their purposes and planned observations. The user can compare both sites, add a plan to document their geological relationship, and save the briefing with its images and structured data. The result records where to look, why it matters, and what remains to be checked.

For example, the saved demo plan links a Skinner Ridge image to documenting outcrop context and requesting a wider view. A Wildcat Ridge image is linked to inspecting grain texture and requesting a close-up with scale. Both sites are connected by a planned observation of their geological relationship.

Design and intended impact

Mission Lens uses XR to connect a map-based plan with the physical actions of looking around, pointing, and framing a view. Users save photographs with selected observation purposes, planned next observations, and unresolved questions; the record also identifies references opened during the session. The intended benefit is a briefing that another person can review without having participated in the XR session.

NASA/JPL's OnSight provides a precedent for using immersive views to support rover-science planning. JPL (2016) (https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/mixed-reality-technology-brings-mars-to-earth/). Research on virtual navigation found real-world transfer after both immersive VR and desktop learning. Hejtmanek et al. (2020) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31972540/). These findings motivate testing embodied preparation in Mission Lens: whether looking around and framing observations helps users remember spatial context and scientific intent. Improved learning remains a hypothesis to evaluate with identical-information Quest and desktop tasks.

Longer term, the aim is helmet-mounted AR that connects the pre-excursion briefing to observations in the field. That would require separate work on spatial registration, display legibility, power constraints, and operational safety.

NASA observations, derived calculations, and hypothetical mission plans are kept distinct. A panorama capture records a view of existing imagery; selecting a close-up adds an observation to the plan. Regional spectral data provide context rather than a ranking of individual outcrops.

Data and technology

MRO HiRISE imagery and terrain support the spatial map and derived slope and visibility layers. CRISM provides regional spectral context. Mars 2020 panoramas, sampling records, and WATSON close-ups connect that orbital view to rover observations.

The application uses Unity 6, C#, URP, OpenXR, and XR Hands, targeting Meta Quest 3. Python with NumPy, Rasterio, Pillow, and OpenCV processes the data; FFmpeg produces the demo.

Current validation and next steps

Editor checks cover the observation workflow, record retention, saving, and loading. The exported demo plan was checked for consistent links between images, purposes, and planned observations. Reproducible audits examined the terrain extract, visibility calculations, panorama registration workflow, and NASA sample records.

Earlier builds ran on Quest 3; the new camera and observation-plan workflow have been checked in the Editor only. The demonstration uses scripted input through the app’s normal controls.

The prototype has not been validated for operational navigation or improved human performance. The next evaluation will test whether another person can identify the locations, purposes, and unresolved questions from a saved briefing, followed by a Quest-versus-desktop comparison using identical information.
